title: Sequences and infinite series
subtitle: When can infinitely many additions produce a finite total?
prerequisites: Definite and improper integrals from chapters 11 and 14
Loops, arrays, and numerical error from chapter 3
objectives: Distinguish a sequence limit from convergence of its series of partial sums.
Use monotonicity and bounds to prove convergence.
Evaluate geometric and telescoping series and estimate their tails.
Apply the divergence, integral, and comparison tests with their hypotheses.

sections.title: A sequence is a function on the counting numbers
paragraphs: A sequence assigns a real number $a_n$ to each positive integer $n$. Its domain is discrete: $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, and so on. The index records position, not necessarily time. In a savings model it might count months; in a numerical algorithm it counts iterations. The values retain their physical units, while the index itself is a dimensionless count. Unless another starting index is stated, this chapter begins at $n=1$.

To say $a_n$ converges to $L$ means that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a positive integer $N$ such that $|a_n-L|<\varepsilon$ for every $n\ge N$. The word every matters. Some terms getting close to $L$ is insufficient if other arbitrarily late terms remain far away. For $a_n=1/n$, choose any integer $N>1/\varepsilon$. Then $n\ge N$ implies $1/n\le 1/N<\varepsilon$. This is a proof of convergence to zero, not an inference from a long decimal table.

The limit laws from functions also apply to sequences when the relevant limits exist, with a nonzero denominator limit required for division. Thus $(3n+2)/(n+5)=(3+2/n)/(1+5/n)$ tends to $3$. A useful bridge is that if $f(x)\to L$ as $x\to\infty$, then $a_n=f(n)\to L$. The converse need not hold: $\sin(\pi n)=0$ at every integer, while $\sin(\pi x)$ has no limit as real $x\to\infty$.

A sequence may diverge by growing without bound, as $n^2$ does, or by oscillating, as $(-1)^n$ does. Being bounded does not alone guarantee convergence. Conversely, convergence guarantees boundedness: after some index the terms lie within one unit of the limit, and finitely many earlier terms have a finite maximum absolute value. Finite initial changes do not affect whether a sequence converges or its eventual limit.

A sequence limit is a claim about the entire tail after one index. For $a_n=(-1)^n/n$, the signs alternate, but $|a_n|=1/n$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, any $N>1/\varepsilon$ ensures $|a_n-0|<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$, so the sequence converges to zero. The oscillation becomes harmless because its amplitude shrinks. In contrast, $(-1)^n$ never settles: even and odd subsequences stay at $1$ and $-1$. Checking these two subsequences proves divergence without needing to enumerate many terms. A graph of the first hundred points may suggest the result, but the all-later-terms condition proves it.

Finite prefixes can be ignored for convergence but not for an actual sum or an initial-condition model. Changing $a_1$ from $1$ to a million leaves the limit of $a_n$ unchanged because the definition allows $N$ beyond the altered term. For a series, changing its first term leaves convergence status unchanged but changes the sum by $999999$. This distinction will matter when formulas are indexed from zero or one. Always write the first few terms before applying a geometric-sum formula; a shifted starting index often changes the numerical answer while leaving the common ratio and convergence condition intact.

A limit law requires the pieces it combines to have limits. It is invalid to say $a_n/b_n\to L/M$ if $b_n\to0$, and even if $b_n$ never equals zero the quotient may grow or oscillate. For example, $(1/n)/(1/n^2)=n$ diverges. Algebraic normalization is more reliable: divide numerator and denominator of $(3n+2)/(n+5)$ by $n$, then apply limit laws to $1/n$. An expression that resembles $0/0$ is a signal to simplify or compare orders, not a numerical value of the limit.

The epsilon definition can be translated into an explicit index budget. For $a_n=5-2/n$, requiring $|a_n-5|<0.01$ means $2/n<0.01$, so any $n>200$ works and $N=201$ is sufficient. This turns an abstract existence claim into a concrete guarantee for all future terms. The chosen $N$ need not be smallest unless the problem asks for it; any valid bound proves convergence. In applications, state whether $\varepsilon$ is an absolute tolerance in the units of $a_n$ or a relative tolerance scaled to a reference value.

A subsequence selects terms with indices $n_1<n_2<\cdots$. If $a_n\to L$, then every subsequence also converges to $L$ because its indices eventually exceed any $N$ from the original epsilon definition. Therefore two subsequences with different limits prove that the full sequence diverges. This is the clean reason even and odd terms settle the fate of $(-1)^n$. The converse is not true when only one subsequence is inspected: an apparently stable run of selected terms can hide other behavior. This cautions against sampling a sequence at convenient indices and inferring a full limit from those alone. The requirement concerns arbitrarily late terms, not merely a long finite plot or a handful of favorable indices.
sections.formula: aₙ → L ⇔ for every ε > 0, some N satisfies n ≥ N ⇒ |aₙ − L| < ε.

sections.title: Monotonicity turns a bound into a limit
paragraphs: A sequence is nondecreasing when $a_{n+1}\ge a_n$ for all $n$, and nonincreasing when the inequality reverses. Either property is called monotonicity. The monotone bounded theorem states that a nondecreasing real sequence bounded above converges; a nonincreasing real sequence bounded below also converges. These are the bounds that oppose its direction of travel. An increasing sequence already has a lower bound at its first term, but that lower bound says nothing about escape to infinity.

Here is the real-number step. An upper bound $U$ of a set is a number at least as large as every element; its supremum $L$ is the least such bound. Completeness of $\mathbb R$ says that every nonempty set of real numbers bounded above has a real supremum. Apply this axiom to the terms of a nondecreasing bounded sequence. For any $\varepsilon>0$, $L-\varepsilon$ cannot be an upper bound, so some $a_N>L-\varepsilon$. Monotonicity yields $L-\varepsilon<a_N\le a_n\le L$ for every $n\ge N$, which is the limit definition. The completeness axiom supplies $L$; the inequality proves that the sequence approaches it.

For a concrete iteration, start $x_1=1$ and define $x_{n+1}=\sqrt{2+x_n}$. Induction shows $1\le x_n\le2$: the interval maps into itself. Also $x_2>x_1$, and the increasing square-root function carries $x_n\ge x_{n-1}$ into $x_{n+1}\ge x_n$. Therefore the sequence has a limit $L\in[1,2]$. Continuity now allows $L=\sqrt{2+L}$, giving $L^2-L-2=0$. Of the roots $2$ and $-1$, only $2$ lies in the permitted interval.

Solving a fixed-point equation was the final step, not the convergence argument. An iteration can have a fixed point while its actual terms fail to approach it. For example, $x_{n+1}=2-x_n$ has the fixed point $1$ but alternates between $0$ and $2$ when started at $0$. Bounds, starting values, and the update rule must all enter the reasoning.

Monotonicity alone does not guarantee a finite limit: $a_n=n$ is increasing and unbounded. Boundedness alone also fails: $a_n=(-1)^n$ is bounded and nonconvergent. The monotone bounded theorem needs both properties at once. Its proof through the supremum explains why the real-number system matters. If an iteration lives in a closed invariant interval and its update preserves order, this theorem can establish convergence before the eventual value is known. Solving the fixed-point equation afterward identifies which possible limit the sequence reaches.

For $x_{n+1}=\sqrt{2+x_n}$ with $x_1=1$, the invariant interval and increasing-step argument above establish convergence before any fixed-point equation is used. Continuity then gives $L=\sqrt{2+L}$; squaring gives candidates $2$ and $-1$, but only $2$ lies in $[1,2]$ and satisfies the original equation. For an optional return after the existing Lesson 2 checkpoint, repeat this proof order for another continuous update: first find an invariant interval and a monotonicity argument, then identify the limit. The fixed-point equation alone cannot supply convergence.

A decreasing bounded example is $a_n=1+1/n$. Its terms decrease because $1/(n+1)<1/n$, and they stay above $1$, so the monotone bounded theorem gives convergence. The explicit formula then identifies the limit $1$. The theorem is more valuable when a closed formula is unavailable. For instance, in many iterative algorithms a carefully chosen invariant interval and a one-step inequality establish monotonicity and boundedness; the update's continuity then determines the limit. When the update is not monotone, a contraction estimate may be more appropriate than forcing a monotone argument.

A bounded recurrence can fail to converge through a cycle. For $x_{n+1}=2-x_n$ started at zero, the terms are $0,2,0,2,\ldots$. The interval $[0,2]$ is invariant and the fixed point equation $L=2-L$ has the solution $1$, but neither subsequence approaches $1$. The missing hypothesis is not boundedness but actual convergence or a theorem that establishes it. This counterexample should be kept in mind whenever a solution begins by writing “let $n\to\infty$” in a recurrence: passing to a limit is legitimate only after convergence has been justified.

Completeness can be expressed through a Cauchy condition: a real sequence converges exactly when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, all sufficiently late terms are within $\varepsilon$ of one another. For $1/n$ this follows because both late terms are close to zero. For $(-1)^n$, arbitrarily late adjacent terms differ by two, so the condition fails. This formulation is useful when the limit is not known in advance; it asks whether the tail settles internally. The monotone bounded theorem is one way to prove that settling property without writing an explicit limit formula. The Cauchy viewpoint will reappear when examining series tails.

theorems.title: Completeness is the hidden step in monotone convergence
theorems.statement: Every bounded nondecreasing sequence of real numbers converges to its least upper bound. A bounded nonincreasing sequence converges to its greatest lower bound.
proof: Let $(s_n)$ be bounded and nondecreasing. The real-number completeness property guarantees that its set of values has a supremum $S$. By definition, every $s_n\le S$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, $S-\varepsilon$ cannot be an upper bound, or $S$ would not be the least upper bound. Therefore some index $N$ satisfies $s_N>S-\varepsilon$. Monotonicity then gives $S-\varepsilon<s_N\le s_n\le S$ for every $n\ge N$, so $|s_n-S|<\varepsilon$. This is the full $\varepsilon$ argument behind the compact phrase “increasing and bounded means convergent.”

For a nonincreasing bounded sequence, apply the same reasoning to $-s_n$ or use the infimum directly. The proof depends on completeness of the real numbers, not merely algebra. For example, rational approximations that increase toward $\sqrt2$ can be bounded in the rational numbers without having a rational limit; the missing least upper bound is irrational. Calculus takes place in a number system where those gaps have been filled.

When applying the theorem to a series with nonnegative terms, take $s_n$ to be its partial sums. They are nondecreasing automatically, so a finite upper bound on all partial sums proves convergence. The individual terms tending to zero gives no such upper bound: harmonic partial sums keep growing. Conversely, if positive partial sums are unbounded, their monotonicity forces divergence to $+\infty$ rather than oscillation.

sections.title: Series are limits of accumulated totals
paragraphs: Given terms $a_n$, define the $N$th partial sum $S_N=a_1+\cdots+a_N$. The infinite series $\sum a_n$ converges to $S$ exactly when the sequence $S_N$ converges to a finite real number $S$. Thus a series introduces a second sequence: the running totals. Terms can shrink while running totals grow without bound. For nonnegative terms, the partial sums are nondecreasing, so the monotone bounded theorem says that the series converges exactly when those partial sums are bounded above.

A necessary condition for convergence is $a_n\to0$. Indeed, $a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$, and if both partial-sum sequences tend to $S$ their difference tends to zero. This gives the divergence test: if the terms do not tend to zero, the series diverges. If the terms do tend to zero, the test gives no conclusion. The harmonic series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n$ will soon supply the decisive counterexample.

For a geometric series indexed from zero, the terms are $a,ar,ar^2,\ldots$. Multiplying the finite sum by $r$ and subtracting gives $\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}ar^k=a(1-r^N)/(1-r)$, provided $r\ne1$. If $|r|<1$, then $r^N\to0$ and the sum is $a/(1-r)$. For nonzero $a$ and $|r|\ge1$, the terms fail the necessary condition; this includes both endpoints $r=1$ and $r=-1$. When $a=0$ every term is zero regardless of $r$.

A telescoping series instead exposes cancellation between neighboring terms. Since $1/[n(n+1)]=1/n-1/(n+1)$, its first $N$ terms sum to $1-1/(N+1)$. Writing a finite partial sum before cancelling avoids ambiguous manipulation of infinite expressions. Taking the limit gives total $1$. The remainder after $N$ terms is exactly $1/(N+1)$, even though the next term is the much smaller $1/[(N+1)(N+2)]$.

For any convergent series define its tail or remainder $R_N=S-S_N$. It is the sum of all omitted terms, not just the next term. In a model where terms measure energy in joules, both partial sums and remainders measure joules. A numerical stopping rule must control this entire tail in the required units.

A series is never literally formed by completing infinitely many additions one after another. It is defined by the limit of finite partial sums. This order of definition protects algebraic manipulations: first derive an identity for $S_N$, then take $N\to\infty$ if that limit exists. For a geometric series with $|r|<1$, the finite identity $S_N=a(1-r^N)/(1-r)$ shows both the sum $a/(1-r)$ and exact tail $ar^N/(1-r)$. The tail formula turns convergence into a practical stopping rule when $a$ and $r$ are known.

The term test is one-way. If $\sum a_n$ converges, then $a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}\to0$. The converse fails because small positive terms can accumulate forever. For the harmonic series, each term becomes tiny but the grouped blocks still contribute at least one half. A useful habit is to check $a_n\to0$ first: failure proves divergence immediately; success merely permits further tests. Do not call it “the convergence test” without that qualification. The same subtlety appears in numerical integration, where a small rate over an infinite domain need not yield a finite total.

The geometric series has several boundary cases. If $r=1$ and $a
e0$, every term equals $a$ and the partial sums $S_N=Na$ diverge linearly. If $r=-1$ and $a
e0$, partial sums alternate between two values. If $|r|>1$ and $a
e0$, term magnitudes grow. If $a=0$, the series is identically zero for every $r$, so statements such as “converges exactly when $|r|<1$” need the nonzero-$a$ qualification. For negative $r\in(-1,0)$, the partial sums oscillate around their limit with shrinking amplitude. A plot makes that pattern visible, while the finite formula proves it.

The remainder is a whole tail, not the first omitted term. For $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/[n(n+1)]$, the $(N+1)$st term is about $1/N^2$, but the entire remainder is $1/(N+1)$, about $1/N$. For a geometric series with ratio $0.6$, the omitted tail is the first omitted term divided by $1-0.6$, or $2.5$ times that term. Using only the next term as an error estimate is valid for some alternating-series conditions developed later, but not for arbitrary positive series. Name the theorem or exact formula behind any stopping claim.

For a series, the Cauchy condition applies to partial sums: every sufficiently late block sum $a_{N+1}+\cdots+a_M$ must be small, uniformly for all $M>N$. The necessary term condition tests only a block of length one, so it is weaker. In the harmonic series, individual late terms are small but sufficiently long late blocks have substantial total. For a positive series, bounding the entire tail is exactly the practical version of this condition. An exact geometric or telescoping remainder is therefore more than a computational convenience; it exhibits the required control of all future contributions.

A series is not merely a sequence with plus signs. Its object is the sequence of partial sums $S_N=\sum_{n=1}^N a_n$, and convergence means that $S_N$ approaches a finite number as $N$ grows. The necessary condition $a_n\to0$ follows because $a_N=S_N-S_{N-1}$ and both partial sums approach the same limit. The converse fails: for the harmonic series $a_n=1/n$ tends to zero, but the partial sums grow without bound. A useful geometric explanation groups terms into blocks: from $n=2^{k-1}+1$ through $2^k$, there are $2^{k-1}$ terms each at least $1/2^k$, so each block adds at least $1/2$. Infinitely many such blocks force unbounded growth. This argument shows why small individual contributions need not have a small accumulated total.
sections.formula: Σ aₙ = S means lim as N → ∞ of S_N = S; R_N = S − S_N.

sections.title: Integral tests and the boundary at p = 1
paragraphs: Suppose $f$ is positive, continuous, and nonincreasing on $[1,\infty)$, and $a_n=f(n)$. The integral test states that $\sum a_n$ and the improper integral $\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx$ either both converge or both diverge. The same conclusion holds if these assumptions begin at some later integer: a finite prefix cannot change convergence. The test compares existence of a finite total, not equality of the integral and the series.

Here is the geometric reason. On each unit interval a decreasing graph lies between rectangles whose heights are its endpoint values. For a convergent positive series this gives $\int_{N+1}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx\le R_N\le\int_N^{\infty}f(x)\,dx$. Summing the finite rectangle inequalities and then taking limits proves these bounds and the convergence equivalence. The required positivity prevents cancellation from invalidating this particular comparison.

Apply the test to $f(x)=x^{-p}$ for $p>0$. The antiderivative when $p\ne1$ is $x^{1-p}/(1-p)$. Its improper integral converges precisely when $p>1$. At $p=1$ the antiderivative is $\ln x$, which grows without bound. Thus the p-series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n^p$ converges exactly for $p>1$; for $p\le0$ its terms do not even tend to zero. The endpoint $p=1$ must be examined separately from the power antiderivative.

The harmonic terms $1/n$ approach zero, yet their sum diverges. Another proof groups the terms with indices $2^{k-1}+1$ through $2^k$. Each group has $2^{k-1}$ terms, each at least $1/2^k$, so each group contributes at least $1/2$. Arbitrarily many such groups force the partial sums above every bound. A plot can look nearly flat because logarithmic growth is slow; its appearance cannot overturn this argument.

For $p>1$ the integral bounds give $(N+1)^{1-p}/(p-1)\le R_N\le N^{1-p}/(p-1)$. With $p=2$ and $N=100$, the tail lies between $1/101$ and $1/100$. The $101$st term is less than $0.0001$, but the full omitted amount is about $0.01$. This explains why stopping merely when an individual term looks small can substantially understate the error.

The integral test rests on a monotone comparison between rectangles and area. If $f$ is positive and decreasing, each term $f(n)$ is the height of a left rectangle on $[n,n+1]$, so it exceeds the area under $f$ there; $f(n+1)$ is a right height and lies below the area. Summing these inequalities and then taking limits traps the tail $R_N$ between improper integrals beginning at $N+1$ and $N$. The positivity makes all partial sums monotone; the decrease establishes the rectangle ordering. If $f$ oscillates sharply or changes sign, the quoted inequalities need not hold even if some related integral happens to converge.

The p-series threshold can be remembered through how quickly an infinite tail shrinks. For $p=2$, $R_N$ lies between $1/(N+1)$ and $1/N$, so $1000$ terms give an upper bound of $0.001$ (at most), while $1001$ terms make this displayed bound strictly below $0.001$. For $p=3$, the upper bound is $1/(2N^2)$, which shrinks much faster. For $p=1$, no finite upper bound of this form exists because the harmonic total diverges. The exact numerical sum of a p-series may be difficult, but convergence and a useful error certificate often follow from the integral comparison alone.

A finite prefix cannot change convergence. If $f$ is eventually decreasing but has a few irregular early values, start the integral test at an index beyond them. Prove the tail converges or diverges, then add the finite prefix. This is an instance of a general principle: convergence is a tail property, while the final sum depends on every term. The exact lower and upper remainder bounds use the index where monotonicity begins and must be shifted accordingly. Copying a bound indexed from one onto a series starting at zero can create an off-by-one numerical error.

The integral test does not say $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f(n)=\int_1^{\infty}f(x)\,dx$. For $f(x)=1/x^2$, the improper integral from $1$ to infinity is $1$, while the series sum is greater than $1$ because its first term is $1$ and the remaining terms are positive. The test compares convergence and bounds the tail; it does not replace discrete accumulation with continuous accumulation exactly. The difference between sum and integral may remain significant even when both converge. Use the correct object when answering a modeled count of discrete cycles.

The harmonic grouping proof can be indexed carefully. The block from $n=2^{k-1}+1$ through $2^k$ contains $2^{k-1}$ terms. Every denominator is at most $2^k$, so each term is at least $1/2^k$ and the block contributes at least $1/2$. After $K$ blocks the partial sum is at least $1+K/2$, which grows without bound. The argument uses positive terms; no cancellation can offset those blocks. It also shows why looking at the first million terms can be deceptive: the partial sum grows only logarithmically, but it keeps growing indefinitely.

The integral remainder bounds have an asymmetry of one index because a decreasing function sits between left and right rectangles. After retaining terms through $N$, the omitted series begins at $N+1$. The lower integral begins at $N+1$, while the upper begins at $N$. For $p=2$ and $N=100$, this yields $1/101\le R_{100}\le1/100$. Reversing the bounds or using the next term as the upper bound would contradict the geometry. A sketch of the first omitted rectangle against the curve can make the index convention memorable.

sections.title: Comparison transfers known behavior
paragraphs: The direct comparison test is an order argument for nonnegative terms. If $0\le a_n\le b_n$ eventually and $\sum b_n$ converges, then $\sum a_n$ converges. Its partial sums are bounded by a finite initial contribution plus the comparison total. If instead $0\le b_n\le a_n$ eventually and $\sum b_n$ diverges, then $\sum a_n$ diverges. Being below a divergent series or above a convergent one gives no conclusion.

For example, $0<1/(n^2+3)\le1/n^2$, so its series converges. Conversely, $n/(n^2+1)\ge1/(2n)$ for $n\ge1$, since $n^2+1\le2n^2$. Its series diverges by comparison with one half of the harmonic series. The inequality direction is the essential step; resemblance alone is not a proof.

Limit comparison can formalize that resemblance. For eventually positive $a_n$ and $b_n$, if $a_n/b_n\to c$ for a finite $c>0$, then their series have the same convergence behavior. Eventually $c/2<a_n/b_n<3c/2$, so direct comparison applies in both directions. A ratio limit of zero or infinity does not give this two-way conclusion. For rational expressions, comparing their leading powers often provides an efficient positive reference series.

A practical investigation begins by naming the terms and their index range, checking the necessary zero limit, and looking for a finite-sum identity. If those do not settle it, positivity may permit comparison or an integral. Record which hypotheses were checked and what tail bound, if any, was obtained. Convergence alone does not say how many terms give a requested accuracy. The next chapter develops further tests for signs and faster-growing expressions.

For a rational term, leading powers often suggest the comparison but do not complete it. Consider $a_n=(4n^2+1)/(n^3+7)$, which behaves like $4/n$. Compute $a_n/(1/n)=n(4n^2+1)/(n^3+7)\to4$. Because the positive limit is finite and nonzero, limit comparison with the harmonic series proves divergence. Simply dropping the lower-order terms without a limit or inequality would be a heuristic. The ratio calculation shows precisely why the omitted terms do not change convergence.

Direct comparison is sometimes simpler than a limit. Since $0<1/(n^2+4n)\le1/n^2$ for $n\ge1$, the series converges. But an upper comparison can also give a tail bound: $R_N\le\sum_{n>N}1/n^2\le\int_N^{\infty}x^{-2}\,dx=1/N$. Thus $N=1000$ suffices for an upper bound of $0.001$. A better comparison may improve the bound, but the displayed one is already a valid certificate. State whether $N$ gives $\le$ or $<$ the requested tolerance; the distinction can shift the smallest integer by one.

The reverse directions are inconclusive. If $0\le a_n\le1/n$ and $\sum1/n$ diverges, $a_n$ could still be $1/n^2$ and converge. If $a_n\ge1/n^2$ and $\sum1/n^2$ converges, $a_n$ could be $1/n$ and diverge. An inequality proves convergence when the unknown series lies below a convergent majorant, and proves divergence when it lies above a divergent minorant. Remember the logical direction by imagining the area under nonnegative bars: being under a finite roof limits the total; being above an infinite floor forces growth.

Limit comparison requires eventual positivity. If terms change sign, their ratio to a positive reference may have a limit but direct positive-term comparison no longer controls cancellation. Later tests distinguish absolute and conditional convergence. Here, when $a_n\ge0$, a finite positive ratio $c$ means that beyond some index the terms are trapped between fixed positive multiples of $b_n$. Thus both totals either stay bounded or grow without bound together. The proof uses inequalities, not a vague claim that two formulas “look similar.”

A comparison proof can sometimes be sharpened into an error guarantee. If $0\le a_n\le b_n$ and a reference tail $B_N=\sum_{n>N}b_n$ is known, then the unknown remainder satisfies $0\le R_N\le B_N$. This turns the same inequality that proves convergence into a stopping rule. For $a_n=1/(n^2+4n)$, comparison with $1/n^2$ gives $R_N\le1/N$ through the integral-test bound. The estimate may be conservative, but it is defensible without knowing the exact sum. If terms are signed, this direct nonnegative-tail argument no longer applies in the same form.

sections.title: Telescoping gives an exact tail, not just a decimal
paragraphs: The infinite series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n(n+1)}$ looks like a p-series, but partial fractions reveal a stronger structure: $\frac{1}{n(n+1)}=\frac1n-\frac{1}{n+1}$. Its $N$th partial sum is $S_N=(1-\frac12)+(\frac12-\frac13)+\cdots+(\frac1N-\frac{1}{N+1})=1-\frac{1}{N+1}$. Every interior fraction cancels.

Taking $N\to\infty$ gives total sum $1$. The remaining tail after $N$ terms is exactly $R_N=1-S_N=1/(N+1)$. For $N=99$ the sum is $0.99$ and the error is exactly $0.01$. To guarantee error below $0.001$, require $1/(N+1)<0.001$, so $N\ge1000$ suffices. This is a term-budget decision, not a guess from a plotted sequence.

Each term is positive, so $S_N$ increases; the exact expression shows it stays below $1$. Monotone bounded partial sums therefore converge, and their formula identifies the limit. The $n$th term tending to zero is necessary but not the reason the total converges: the harmonic terms $1/n$ also tend to zero while their partial sums diverge. Cancellation in the partial-fraction expression is what makes this series transparent.

When telescoping a different series, write out at least several partial sums before canceling. Endpoint terms are easy to lose, and a shifted starting index changes the answer. State the tail with the same index convention used for the partial sum; an off-by-one error can spoil an otherwise correct tolerance calculation.

Telescoping is easiest to audit with a partial-sum ledger. For $\sum_{n=1}^{N}[1/n-1/(n+1)]$, write the first two and last two pairs. Each interior reciprocal appears once positive and once negative, leaving $1-1/(N+1)$. Starting at $n=2$ would leave $1/2-1/(N+1)$, so the infinite sum would be $1/2$. The first index is part of the problem data. A neat cancellation pattern does not excuse omitting that initial term.

For $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/[(n+1)(n+2)]$, partial fractions give $1/(n+1)-1/(n+2)$. The $N$th sum is $1/2-1/(N+2)$, tending to $1/2$. Its tail after $N$ terms is $1/(N+2)$. This shifted example is a useful off-by-one test for an algorithm that generates partial sums. If it reports $1$ instead, it has silently started at $n=0$ or used the wrong endpoint. Exact finite identities are especially valuable for testing code because they supply a reference at every $N$, not just in the limit.

A more subtle telescope appears in $1/[n(n+2)]$. Partial fractions give $(1/2)(1/n-1/(n+2))$. After $N$ terms, two initial terms and two final terms remain: $S_N=(1/2)[1+1/2-1/(N+1)-1/(N+2)]$. The sum is therefore $3/4$ and the tail is $(1/2)[1/(N+1)+1/(N+2)]$. Two strands cancel separately because the shift is two rather than one. Writing a few finite terms reveals this structure more safely than trying to cancel an infinite expression at once.

An exact tail can be turned into an integer budget. For the basic telescope $R_N=1/(N+1)$, demanding $R_N\le0.001$ means $N+1\ge1000$, so $N\ge999$ suffices. Demanding the strict inequality $R_N<0.001$ requires $N+1>1000$, so $N\ge1000$. Many examples state “below” and mean strict inequality. Attending to that word prevents an off-by-one error at the threshold. The physical units of the remainder are the units of the individual terms, such as joules in the repeated-transfer example.

Finite changes do not affect convergence classification, but they do affect a numerical tail if the cutoff falls before the changes end. Suppose a sequence is altered at its first ten indices. For $N\ge10$, the tail after $N$ is unchanged; for $N<10$, it is not. This simple fact matters when a model has an introductory cycle with a different rule before settling into a geometric pattern. Start the geometric calculation at the first index where the fixed ratio actually holds, and add the earlier contributions separately. A formula extrapolated backward can give a neat but incorrect total.

Telescoping can coexist with positivity even though its algebra uses subtraction. The terms $1/n-1/(n+1)$ are positive because $1/n$ is decreasing. Their finite sums therefore increase, while the cancellation formula keeps them below one. This gives both a conceptual convergence proof and an exact value. In other telescopes, individual terms may have signs or cancellations across several indices; then one must check the partial sums directly. Never cancel an unbounded collection of symbols before writing a finite identity, because the limit of the remaining boundary terms is the very question under study.

examples.title: A repeated energy transfer
examples.problem: A device transfers $12$ joules on its first cycle and $60\%$ of the preceding transfer on each later cycle. Find the idealized total and a cycle count giving less than $0.1$ joule of omitted transfer.
steps: The $n$th transfer is $a_n=12(0.6)^{n-1}$ joules for $n\ge1$. The constant ratio assumption is the model, and $|0.6|<1$ permits the geometric formula.
After $N$ cycles, $S_N=12[1-(0.6)^N]/0.4=30[1-(0.6)^N]$ joules. The infinite total is $30$ joules.
The exact omitted total is $R_N=30(0.6)^N$. We need $(0.6)^N<1/300$. Taking logarithms and dividing by negative $\ln(0.6)$ reverses the inequality: $N>\ln(1/300)/\ln(0.6)$, about $11.17$.
Choose $N=12$. Direct substitution gives $R_{12}\approx0.0653035$ joule; at $N=11$ it is about $0.108839$ joule.
examples.answer: The model predicts $30$ joules in total; $12$ cycles are the smallest count meeting the strict $0.1$-joule tail requirement.

examples.title: Similar-looking small terms, different totals
steps: Both term sequences tend to zero, so the divergence test cannot decide either series.
For the first series, $n/(n^2+1)\ge1/(2n)$ for $n\ge1$. The harmonic series diverges, hence so does this larger positive series.
For the second, write $1/[n(n+1)]=1/n-1/(n+1)$. The first $N$ terms telescope to $1-1/(N+1)$.
The second partial sum tends to $1$. For $N=100$ it is $100/101\approx0.990099$, leaving $1/101\approx0.009901$.
examples.answer: The first series diverges; the second converges to $1$. Small terms are a necessary condition, not a sufficient condition.

examples.title: An explicit epsilon index
examples.problem: Prove that $a_n=5-2/n$ converges to $5$ and give an index for $\varepsilon=0.01$.
steps: The distance to $5$ is $|a_n-5|=2/n$.
Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose an integer $N>2/\varepsilon$. Then every $n\ge N$ satisfies $2/n\le2/N<\varepsilon$.
For $\varepsilon=0.01$, $N=201$ works because every $n\ge201$ exceeds $200$.
examples.answer: The limit is $5$; $N=201$ guarantees error below $0.01$.

examples.title: A bounded cycle defeats a fixed-point guess
steps: The sequence begins $0,2,0,2$ and repeats.
The even subsequence is constantly $2$ while the odd subsequence is constantly $0$, so no single limit exists.
The update has fixed point $1$, but the actual orbit does not approach it.
examples.answer: The bounded sequence diverges by oscillation.

examples.title: A geometric tail is larger than its next term
examples.problem: Sum $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}3(1/2)^{n-1}$ and find the remainder after five terms.
steps: The first term is $3$ and ratio $1/2$, so the infinite sum is $3/(1-1/2)=6$.
The first five terms sum to $6[1-(1/2)^5]=6-3/16$.
The omitted tail is $6(1/2)^5=3/16$, while the sixth term alone is $3/32$.
examples.answer: Total $6$; after five terms the exact remainder is $3/16$.

examples.title: An integral-test tail certificate
examples.problem: For $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n^2$, bound the remainder after $N=100$ terms.
steps: The function $f(x)=x^{-2}$ is positive, continuous, and decreasing for $x\ge1$.
Because $f$ decreases, $\int_n^{n+1}f(x)\,dx\le f(n)\le\int_{n-1}^{n}f(x)\,dx$. Sum over $n\ge N+1$ and pass to the limit to bracket the omitted tail.
Integral-test remainder bounds give $\int_{101}^{\infty}x^{-2}\,dx\le R_{100}\le\int_{100}^{\infty}x^{-2}\,dx$.
The integrals are $1/101$ and $1/100$.

examples.title: Leading powers require a limit comparison
steps: The terms are positive. Compare with $b_n=1/n$, the harmonic reference.
The ratio $a_n/b_n=n(4n^2+1)/(n^3+7)$ tends to $4$.
A finite positive ratio transfers divergence from the harmonic series.

examples.title: A two-step telescope
examples.problem: Find $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/[n(n+2)]$ and its exact remainder after $N$ terms.
steps: Partial fractions give $1/[n(n+2)]=(1/2)(1/n-1/(n+2))$.
Finite cancellation leaves $S_N=(1/2)[1+1/2-1/(N+1)-1/(N+2)]$.
Taking $N\to\infty$ gives $3/4$; subtracting $S_N$ gives $R_N=(1/2)[1/(N+1)+1/(N+2)]$.

misconceptions: “A bounded sequence must converge.” The sequence $(-1)^n$ stays in $[-1,1]$ but alternates forever. Monotonicity is an additional hypothesis in the monotone bounded theorem.
“Once the next term is tiny, the total is accurate.” The remaining infinitely many terms can outweigh that term, and the series may even diverge. Control a proven tail bound.

lab.title: Partial sums and certified tails
lab.description: Compare a $p$-series with a telescoping series over integer indices. The horizontal axis is $N$, a dimensionless count; the vertical axes are dimensionless totals or tails. Edit p and Nmax. Tail bounds appear only when $p>1$, where they are mathematically justified.
tasks: Before running, predict whether the next term of the p-series or its plotted tail upper bound is larger when p = 2 and Nmax = 100. Explain why.
Change p to 1 and compare Nmax = 100 with Nmax = 1000. Does the modest growth justify declaring convergence? Use the harmonic grouping proof.
Set p = 1.1 and Nmax = 1000. Explain why the proven tail bound remains large despite decreasing terms.
Try Nmax = 0 and explain the validation error. Why would an arbitrary extension of the tail formula to p = 1 be invalid?
lab.expected: With the default p = 2 and Nmax = 100, the p-series partial sum is approximately 1.6349839001848923. Its tail lies in $[1/101,1/100]$, or approximately $[0.009900990099009901,0.01]$. The telescoping partial sum is approximately 0.99009900990099 and its exact tail is $1/101$. The p-series bounds follow from integrating $x^{-2}$; the telescoping value follows from its finite-sum identity.

exercises.question: Prove that $a_n = 5 - 2/n$ converges to 5 using the definition.
exercises.hint: Choose $N$ so that $2/N<\varepsilon$.
exercises.solution: Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose an integer $N>2/\varepsilon$. For $n\ge N$, $|a_n-5|=2/n\le2/N<\varepsilon$; hence $a_n\to5$.

exercises.question: What is the smallest positive integer $N$ for which $1/n<0.02$ for every $n\ge N$?
exercises.hint: Solve $1/n<0.02$ with the inequality strict.
exercises.solution: The condition is $n>50$. It fails at $n=50$ and holds thereafter, so the smallest choice is $N=51$.

exercises.question: Does $a_n=(-1)^n/n$ converge?
exercises.hint: Bound $|a_n|$ by $1/n$.
exercises.solution: Because $|a_n-0|=1/n\to0$, for any $\varepsilon>0$ choose $N>1/\varepsilon$; then $n\ge N$ gives $|a_n|<\varepsilon$. Thus $a_n\to0$.

exercises.question: Does $a_n=(-1)^n$ converge?
exercises.hint: Compare the even and odd subsequences.
exercises.solution: No. The even subsequence is constantly $1$, while the odd subsequence is constantly $-1$; a convergent sequence cannot have different subsequential limits.

exercises.question: Give $N$ for $|5-2/n-5|<0.01$ for all $n\ge N$.
exercises.hint: Solve $2/n<0.01$ and respect the strict inequality.
exercises.solution: The inequality is $2/n<0.01$, or $n>200$. Thus $N=201$ is the first integer that works for every later term.

exercises.question: A sequence is nonincreasing and satisfies $3 \le a_n \le 8$. Must it converge, and must its limit equal 3?
exercises.hint: Use bounded monotonicity for existence; test whether the lower bound determines the limit.
exercises.solution: The sequence converges because it is nonincreasing and bounded below by $3$. Its limit lies in $[3,8]$ but need not be $3$: $a_n=6$ meets all assumptions and tends to $6$.

exercises.question: Is $a_n=1+1/n$ decreasing and bounded below? What is its limit?
exercises.hint: Compare $1/(n+1)$ with $1/n$.
exercises.solution: Since $1/(n+1)<1/n$, the sequence decreases. Also $a_n>1$ and $1/n\to0$, so $a_n\to1$.

exercises.question: Can a bounded recurrence with a fixed point fail to converge?
exercises.hint: Try $x_{n+1}=2-x_n$ from an initial value other than the fixed point.
exercises.solution: Yes. For $x_{n+1}=2-x_n$ with $x_0=0$, the bounded sequence is $0,2,0,2,\ldots$ and does not converge, although $1$ is a fixed point.

exercises.question: Why does an increasing sequence bounded above converge?
exercises.hint: Let $L$ be the supremum and use its defining property.
exercises.solution: Let $L=\sup\{a_n:n\ge1\}$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, some $a_N>L-\varepsilon$. Monotonicity gives $L-\varepsilon<a_N\le a_n\le L$ for $n\ge N$, hence $a_n\to L$.

exercises.question: What interval is invariant under $x\mapsto\sqrt{2+x}$ for $x\in[1,2]$?
exercises.hint: Check the endpoint values of the increasing map $F(x)=\sqrt{2+x}$.
exercises.solution: The map $F(x)=\sqrt{2+x}$ is increasing on $[1,2]$. Thus $F([1,2])=[\sqrt3,2]\subseteq[1,2]$, so the interval is invariant.

exercises.question: Evaluate $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 3(-1/2)^{n-1}$, and find the absolute error after five terms.
exercises.hint: Identify the first term and ratio; the tail starts at exponent $5$.
exercises.solution: The geometric series has $a=3$ and $r=-1/2$, giving sum $a/(1-r)=2$. Its remainder after five terms is $ar^5/(1-r)=-1/16$, so the absolute error is $1/16$ and $S_5=33/16$.

exercises.question: Find the sum of $\sum_{n=0}^\infty 5\left(\frac13\right)^n$.
exercises.hint: Use the geometric sum with first term $5$.
exercises.solution: With first term $5$ and ratio $1/3$, the sum is $5/(1-1/3)=15/2$.

exercises.question: Find the sum of $\sum_{n=1}^\infty 5\left(\frac13\right)^n$.
exercises.hint: The first term is $5/3$, since the index starts at $1$.
exercises.solution: Starting at $n=1$ makes the first term $5/3$. The sum is $(5/3)/(1-1/3)=5/2$.

exercises.question: For $\sum_{n=1}^\infty 3\left(\frac12\right)^{n-1}$, find the tail after five terms.
exercises.hint: The omitted terms start at exponent $5$; use the geometric tail formula.
exercises.solution: The first omitted term is $3(1/2)^5$, with ratio $1/2$. Thus $R_5=3(1/2)^5/(1-1/2)=3/16$.

exercises.question: Prove that convergence of $\sum a_n$ implies $a_n\to0$, then give a counterexample showing that the converse is false. Apply the necessary condition to $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(2n+1)/(n+3)$ and justify a convergence or divergence decision without seeking a sum formula.
exercises.hint: Express a term as $a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$, then test the converse with a familiar series.
exercises.solution: If $S_n\to S$, then $a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}\to S-S=0$. The converse fails: $1/n\to0$ but $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n$ diverges. For $a_n=(2n+1)/(n+3)$, dividing numerator and denominator by $n$ gives $a_n\to2$. Since the terms do not tend to zero, the series diverges by the contrapositive of the necessary condition. No partial-sum formula is needed.

exercises.question: Determine the convergence behavior of $\sum (n+1)/(n+2)$ and $\sum 1/\sqrt n$.
exercises.hint: Check term limits first; identify the second sum as a $p$-series.
exercises.solution: For $(n+1)/(n+2)$, the terms tend to $1$, so the series diverges. The second is $\sum n^{-1/2}$, a divergent $p$-series because $p=1/2\le1$.

exercises.question: Classify $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^{3/2}}$.
exercises.hint: Compare the exponent with the $p=1$ threshold.
exercises.solution: This is a $p$-series with $p=3/2>1$, so it converges.

exercises.question: Classify $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac1{\sqrt n}$.
exercises.hint: Write $1/\sqrt n=n^{-1/2}$ and apply the $p$-series criterion.
exercises.solution: This is a $p$-series with $p=1/2\le1$, so it diverges.

exercises.question: Bound the tail of $\sum \frac1{n^2}$ after $N=100$.
exercises.hint: Use integral-test bounds with lower limits $100$ and $101$.
exercises.solution: For the decreasing function $x^{-2}$, $\int_{101}^{\infty}x^{-2}\,dx\le R_{100}\le\int_{100}^{\infty}x^{-2}\,dx$. Evaluating gives $1/101\le R_{100}\le1/100$.

exercises.question: Why does $\int_1^\infty x^{-2}\,dx$ not equal $\sum \frac1{n^2}$?
exercises.hint: The integral test compares totals; compare the first term with the integral.
exercises.solution: The integral is $\int_1^{\infty}x^{-2}\,dx=1$. The series has first term $1$ and further positive terms, so $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n^{-2}>1$. The test establishes convergence and bounds, not equality.

exercises.question: Prove convergence of $\sum 1/(n^2+4n)$, and give a sufficient $N$ for its omitted positive tail to be at most 0.001.
exercises.hint: Compare terms and omitted tails with $1/n^2$.
exercises.solution: For $n\ge1$, $0<1/(n^2+4n)\le1/n^2$, so comparison with the convergent $p=2$ series proves convergence. The omitted tail obeys $R_N\le\sum_{n>N}n^{-2}\le\int_N^{\infty}x^{-2}\,dx=1/N$; hence $N=1000$ suffices.

exercises.question: Use limit comparison to classify $\sum \frac{4n^2+1}{n^3+7}$.
exercises.hint: Compare with $b_n=1/n$ using a ratio limit.
exercises.solution: With $b_n=1/n$, $\frac{(4n^2+1)/(n^3+7)}{b_n}=\frac{n(4n^2+1)}{n^3+7}\to4$. The positive finite limit transfers the harmonic series divergence.

exercises.question: Classify $\sum \frac1{n^2+4n}$ by direct comparison.
exercises.hint: Compare each positive term with $1/n^2$.
exercises.solution: For $n\ge1$, $n^2+4n\ge n^2$, so $0<1/(n^2+4n)\le1/n^2$. The comparison series $\sum n^{-2}$ converges because $p=2>1$. Direct comparison therefore proves that the requested series converges.

exercises.question: Classify $\sum \frac{4n^2+1}{n^3+7}$.
exercises.hint: Compare the ratio of terms with that of $1/n$.
exercises.solution: The ratio $\frac{(4n^2+1)/(n^3+7)}{1/n}=\frac{n(4n^2+1)}{n^3+7}\to4>0$. Limit comparison with the divergent harmonic series proves divergence.

exercises.question: Why is being below $1/n$ inconclusive for convergence?
exercises.hint: Find one convergent and one divergent series below $1/n$.
exercises.solution: The series $\sum 1/n^2$ converges and $\sum 1/n$ diverges, although both have terms at most $1/n$. An upper bound by a divergent series decides neither case.

exercises.question: Evaluate $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/[(n+1)(n+2)]$.
exercises.hint: Split each term into $1/(n+1)-1/(n+2)$.

exercises.question: Evaluate $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac1{n(n+2)}$.
exercises.solution: The partial fraction identity gives $S_N=\frac12[1+1/2-1/(N+1)-1/(N+2)]$. The last two terms vanish, leaving $3/4$.

exercises.question: Prove that the partial sums $S_N=\sum_{n=1}^N \frac1{n(n+1)}$ converge without first naming their limit.
exercises.hint: Show the positive partial sums increase and have a finite upper bound.
exercises.solution: Each summand is positive, so $S_N$ increases. Telescoping gives $S_N=1-1/(N+1)<1$, so bounded monotonicity proves convergence; the formula then shows the limit is $1$.

exercises.question: Find $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac1{(n+1)(n+2)}$.
exercises.hint: Telescope the shifted fractions before taking $N\to\infty$.
exercises.solution: The shifted telescope gives $S_N=1/2-1/(N+2)$. As $N\to\infty$, the sum is $1/2$.

exercises.question: Starting with no drug in the body, a repeated treatment adds 80 mg of a drug immediately every six hours, and 60% of the amount present remains just before the next dose. Assuming the pattern continues indefinitely, find the limiting amount immediately after a dose and explain the indexing.
exercises.hint: Add the surviving doses as $80\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(0.6)^k$ immediately after dose $n$.
exercises.solution: After dose $n$, the amount is $80\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(0.6)^k=200[1-(0.6)^n]\,\mathrm{mg}$. Since $(0.6)^n\to0$, the post-dose amount tends to $200\,\mathrm{mg}$. Exponent $0$ represents the fresh dose before decay.

summary: A sequence converges when every sufficiently late term is close to one finite value. Monotonicity and an appropriate bound guarantee such a limit.
A series converges when its partial sums converge; vanishing terms alone do not suffice.
Geometric and telescoping identities can give exact sums and remainders. Positive-term integral and comparison tests prove convergence or divergence, and integral bounds can certify tails.
next: Chapter 16 extends these ideas to alternating signs, absolute convergence, ratio and root tests, and reliable stopping criteria for numerical approximations.
